title: "Collections, Iterators, and Closures"
description: "One key Rust idea, one tiny executable example, the reason it works, and a precise pitfall."
---

## The question

**How do we sum only the odd numbers without managing a mutable index?**

An iterator is a sequence of values consumed through operations such as `filter`, `map`, and `sum`. A closure describes the small decision applied to each item.

## The core rule

Be explicit whether an iterator borrows values (`iter`) or takes them by value (`into_iter`).

## One complete example

Paste these lines into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`, or [use the tested Rust examples project](examples/index.qmd).

~~~rust
fn main() {
    let values = [1, 2, 3, 4];
    let sum: i32 = values.into_iter()
        .filter(|n| *n % 2 == 1)
        .sum();
    println!("{sum}"); // 4
}
~~~

**Walk through it:** `into_iter()` yields each integer. The closure `|n| n % 2 == 1` keeps odd values 1 and 3; `sum()` produces 4. It describes the same sequence of operations as a manual loop.

## Mathematical model — explained with real values

$$
S=\sum_{x\in\{1,3\}}x
$$

**What every symbol means:** `S` is the resulting sum; `Σ` means add; `x` takes each selected odd value in the set `{1,3}`.

**Substitute actual values:** After the filter only values 1 and 3 remain, so `S=1+3=4`, which is exactly the printed result.

## Common misunderstanding

Iterator adapters are lazy until consumed by a terminal operation such as `collect`, `sum`, or a `for` loop. Avoid assuming `map(...)` alone executes side effects immediately.

## Remember it in one sentence

Be explicit whether an iterator borrows values (`iter`) or takes them by value (`into_iter`).

**Official reference:** [The Rust Programming Language / Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch13-02-iterators.html).
